articles.title: Melding om skyting ved barneskole i USA
articles.content:
Minst to personer er sendt til sykehus med ukjent skadeomfang etter at det ble avfyrt skudd på Silver Rail Elementary School i Bend i Oregon.

Personen som skjøt er død, opplyste politiet på en pressekonferanse torsdag ettermiddag lokal tid.

– Vi har ikke noen bekreftelse ennå på hvem som skjøt den mistenkte. Det kan ha vært noen som var til stede. Det dreier seg om flere ofre, sier talskvinne Sheila Miller i politiet i Bend.

Store politistyrker rykket ut til barneskolen etter melding om en aktiv skytter klokka 12.59 lokal tid.

Skolen ligger rundt 160 kilometer sørøst for Portland. I fjor hadde den 459 elever, ifølge tall fra delstatens myndigheter.

articles.title: Bekymringsmelding mot kommunedirektøren i Tromsø
articles.content:
Ledergruppen i Tromsø kommune har sendt en bekymringsmelding mot kommunedirektør Ellen Beate Lundberg.

Til NRK bekrefter ordfører Gunnar Wilhelmsen at de har mottatt bekymringsmeldingen. Han er leder av arbeidsgiverutvalget, som behandler saken.

«Saken følges opp av arbeidsgiverutvalget i tråd med kommunens rutiner. Vi gjennomfører de undersøkelsene som er nødvendige for å få saken tilstrekkelig belyst og vurderer den videre oppfølgingen fortløpende.

Av hensyn til de involverte og den pågående behandlingen ønsker jeg ikke å kommentere sakens innhold eller den konkrete behandlingen i arbeidsgiverutvalget.»

NRK har vært i kontakt med flere av lederne i kommunen, som ikke ønsker å kommentere saken.

Det har ikke lyktes å få en kommentar fra kommunedirektør Lundberg.

Tromsø kommune har nettopp blitt oppført på Robek-lista, og kommunedirektøren har ansvaret for en solid økonomisk prosess.

Fire ledere rundt Ellen Beate Lundberg skal ha levert en bekymringsmelding mot kvinnen som har ansvaret for å få Tromsø ut av Robek-lista.

articles.title: Ungarn får 2,7 milliarder kroner av Norge
articles.content:
Ungarn vil igjen motta EØS-midler fra Norge, melder Ungarns utenriksminister Anita Orban på Facebook.

Forhandlingene om EØS og den norske finansieringsordningen er avsluttet. Signeringen av samarbeidsavtalen for gjennomføring i perioden 2021–2028 vil finne sted om kort tid, skriver Orban.

Norge holdt tilbake EØS-midler på grunn av styret til landets forrige statsminister Viktor Orbán.

Ungarn vil motta 254 millioner euro i EØS-midler. Det tilsvarer 2,7 milliarder norske kroner.

– Avtalen åpner et nytt kapittel i forholdet mellom Norge og Ungarn. Midlene vil komme Ungarns befolkning til gode og støtte opp under Magyar-regjeringens reformer for demokrati, rettsstat og menneskerettigheter, sier den norske utenriksministeren Espen Barth Eide i en pressemelding.

Eide sier norske og ungarske aktører vil samarbeide om prosjekter og tema som pressefrihet, likestilling, grønn omstilling og inkludering av minoriteter i tillegg til tiltak for å bekjempe korrupsjon og desinformasjon.

EØS-avtalen

Det er solid flertall for fortsatt norsk EØS-medlemskap. En meningsmåling fra november 2021 viser at dersom det hadde det vært en ny folkeavstemning om EØS, ville 65,1 prosent stemt ja og 19,4 prosent stemt nei .

Ungarn

Opposisjonspartiet Tisza og partileder Peter Magyar har vunnet valget i Ungarn. Frem til nå har Russland-vennlige Viktor Orbán styrt landet. Det har han gjort siden 2010.

articles.content:

Det seier Joakim Vedeler, redaksjonssjef for Barn og tenåringar i NRK, til Kampanje.

NRK har i staden kjøpt rettane til alle dei 30 episodane av «Rykter» frå buet for 300.000 kroner for å sikre at serien framleis vil vere tilgjengeleg for publikum.

                        Norwegian police said Wednesday that they had arrested five people as part of an investigation into aggravated fraud against a NATO agency.

The people, who were arrested in the region of Bergen in western Norway, are suspected of "over-invoicing" the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) for services provided to NATO ships in Norwegian ports between 2021 and 2025.

The overcharges are more than one million euros ($1.12 million), police said in a statement.

"Defence sector budgets are increasing worldwide, which entails an increased risk of economic crime. This is an area we are monitoring closely," said Marianne Bender, Senior Public Prosecutor at Norway's national economic crime unit.

"If NATO has been defrauded, there will be a tough crackdown," she added.

Romanian and German police have also carried out searches at several companies in Romania and Germany suspected of being linked to the same case, according to the statement.

articles.title: Avviser ny behandling av Frogner-kvinnens erstatningskrav
articles.content:
Borgarting lagmannsrett avviser kravet om en ny vurdering av erstatningskravet i Høiby-saken fra den såkalte Frogner-kvinnen, Det opplyser retten i en pressemelding.

Kvinnen krevde at det sivile kravet skulle behandles som en det av rettssaken mot Høiby i lagmannsretten.

Marius Borg Høiby ble i tingretten dømt til å betale 110.000 kroner til Frogner-kvinnen.

Fornærmede kan kreve fortsatt behandling av kravet etter tvistelovens regler.

Straffesaken mot Marius Borg Høiby

articles.content:

        Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Autumn has arrived in all its glory, and Oslo is ablaze with vibrant colours. But where should photographers go to snap the most dramatic foliage? Our travel editor Marie Peyre has some advice.

There are plenty of deciduous trees within the grounds of Akershus Fortress, so this is a good spot to take pictures of autumn colours. The small cobblestoned street leading up to the Resistance Museum in particular is quite striking this time of year. Look down, as well as up - it's not just the treetops that turn yellow, the ground is also covered in golden leaves.

A popular destination year round, the Vigeland Sculpture Park really comes into its own on a sunny autumn day, when the vivid foliage makes a colourful background for the striking sculptures. Slottsparken, the park behind the Royal Palace, with its grand old trees and extensive lawns, is another good bet.

A stroll along the Akerselva will also reveal many good subjects for photography, as the river winds its way past old mills, neighbourhood parks and hidden fishing spots, under old iron bridges and through many waterfalls. The stretch around the Sawmill Waterfall (Møllerfossene) north of Grünerløkka is particularly picturesque, and from here you can easily continue onto Telthusbakken, Old Aker Church and the Our Saviour Cemetery - all good spots for taking pictures of autumn colours.

For a different perspective on the city, take a hop on, hop off cruise on the Oslofjord - a great opportunity to check out the many islands there, and shoot from the water as well as from land. Hovedøya, the island closest to the mainland, boasts forests, beaches and several interesting buildings, including  the ruins of a Cistercian monastery dating back to 1147. Part of the island is a nature reserve. Ferries depart year round from Aker Brygge.

Want a full day snapping away? Jump on the T-banen and head to Nordmarka - Oslo's main recreational area, only a few minutes from the city centre. Here miles of tracks await, most of them going through forested terrain - another great destination for photographers in search of interesting autumn scenes.

articles.title: Free legal aid for immigrants in Norway faces heavy funding cuts
articles.content:
Add a comment
                                                                                            
                                        
                                                                        
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                
                            
                        
                    
                    
                    
                            
                            The Norwegian government has proposed a 35 million kroner cut to targeted legal aid measures in the 2027 state budget,  which could affect many immigrants and refugees in the country. Photo by Vitaly Gariev on Unsplash
                    
                                            
                            
        
            
            
            
            
        
        Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        What happens when you find yourself up against an unfair landlord, an abusive boss, or face discrimination in Norway? In one of the world’s most expensive countries, financial aid that thousands of immigrants rely on is suddenly under threat.

These organisations are largely supported by public funding, employing specialists, qualified lawyers, and law students to guide people through their cases, including those who have problems with their employer, are at risk of losing their residence permit, or are victims of violence, abuse or discrimination.

However, the government has proposed a 35 million kroner cut to targeted legal aid measures in the 2027 state budget, as multicultural newspaper Utrop reported.

READ MORE: Where to get free immigration advice in Norway

The proposal has caused real worry among advocacy groups who argue that free legal guidance can be crucial to safeguarding people's rights in Norway.

Organisations such as Legal Advice for Women (Juridisk rådgivning for kvinner - JURK) warn that less public funding will directly affect international residents, who often depend on these services for help with work disputes, immigration problems, and discrimination.

"Less money means less legal aid," Susan Arulanantham, General Manager of JURK, told the magazine Advokatbladet. "It is the paradox of this cut: it could hit hardest the very part of our work that ensures we reach the women who face the highest threshold for asking for help."

The Ministry of Justice justified the cut by pointing to recent reforms that expanded eligibility for state-funded lawyers, claiming that fewer people now rely on non-profit services. However, grassroots groups dispute this, saying their caseload has not decreased at all since the law changed, and warning that if the proposal is approved, they will have to take fewer cases or might even have to shut down temporarily.

"We have not seen any drop in inquiries," Georg Schjerven Hansen, head of Kontoret for fri rettshjelp, told Advokatbladet. "The legal reforms involve graded co-payments with the state as creditor, meaning many who may now be covered by the Legal Aid Act still do not dare seek out a private lawyer for fear of unexpected costs."

Jacob Anker Eide, spokesperson for the Legal Aid Alliance (Rettshjelpsalliansen) echoed the concerns: "Those who will be hit by this proposed cut are the worker who has had their wages stolen, the tenant threatened with eviction, social assistance recipients who don't have enough money for food, the grandfather who has been defrauded of his entire pension, asylum seekers, prison inmates, and many others."

Antirasistisk Senter, an anti-racism NGO operating in Norway since 1983, warned on its website: “When legal aid is cut, protection against racism and discrimination is weakened."

The organisation pointed out that even though the government says more people will get free legal aid through the new reforms, discrimination cases will still largely fall outside the system.

“Discrimination cases are still not among the prioritised types of cases under the Legal Aid Act,” the NGO explained.

They also stressed that there is already “a huge unmet need for legal aid among our target groups” and warned of serious consequences if the 2027 state budget passes with less funding for social organisations.

“The government must therefore reverse the proposed cut and ensure that targeted legal aid measures have a predictable framework,” the organisation urged.

articles.content:
Add a comment
                                                                                            
                                        
                                                                        
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                    
                                        
                                            
                                        
                                    
                                
                            
                        
                    
                    
                    
                            
                            Whether you're seeking assistance with family immigration cases, permanent residence permits, or citizenship applications, here's where to look if you need free expert advice. Photo by Amy Hirschi on Unsplash

                        Navigating Norway's immigration laws can be complex. Fortunately, several organisations provide free guidance to people facing immigration challenges.

As is the case in most European countries, immigrants and asylum seekers in Norway are fortunate to have access to a number of organisations dedicated to providing free guidance, support, and legal aid.

Whether you're seeking assistance with asylum claims, family immigration cases, permanent residence permits, or citizenship applications, here's where to look if you need free expert advice and support.

READ MORE: Do you need a lawyer in Norway for work permit or residency problems?

NOAS usually supports people navigating the asylum process in Norway. They specialise in asylum cases and offer legal aid to those whose asylum claims have been rejected by the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) or the Immigration Appeals Board (UNE).

Furthermore, NOAS extends its services to family immigration cases, permanent residence permits, and citizenship matters.

You can contact them via phone at +47 22 36 56 60 or through their email at post@noas.org

Additionally, if you want to book face-to-face assistance, you can visit NOAS's office at Torggata 22, Oslo, during office hours.

Operated by dedicated students in Oslo, Jussbuss is a great resource for people seeking free legal aid, including assistance with immigration-related matters.

Jussbuss accepts new cases and offers guidance on various legal issues through phone consultations (+47 22 84 29 00) or in-person visits during their office hours at Skippergata 23 in Oslo.

They specialise in immigration, labour, debt issues, social security, tenancy, and prison law.

Launched with the objective of empowering immigrants and refugees, SEIF operates as a voluntary organisation committed to providing support and guidance.

With offices across Norway, SEIF offers a number of services, ranging from information dissemination to assistance with complex immigration matters.

Their areas of assistance include issues with the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV), school, work, residence permits, family reunification, financial problems, forced marriage and honour-related violence, coercion, and more.

They have an open-door policy and commitment to confidentiality.

You can find all the contact information for their offices in Oslo, Kristiansand, Ålesund, Trondheim, Bergen, Stavanger, and Tromsø here.

Catering specifically to women, JURK provides free legal assistance on a number of issues, including immigration matters, thereby addressing the often unique needs of female immigrants and asylum seekers. Along with free legal aid, JURK examines women's need for legal assistance, works to improve the legal position of women, and provides practical legal training for law students.

Staffed by students from the University of Bergen Faculty of Law, Jussformidlingen extends its services to people across Norway, leveraging its expertise to offer guidance and assistance on a wide scope of legal issues on civil law, including immigration challenges. It aims to provide free legal aid, meet the public demand for legal assistance, and offer law students practical experience opportunities.

Serving as the umbrella organisation for various student legal aid entities, Gratis Rettshjelp coordinates efforts to provide assistance on various matters, including immigration. It receives approximately 20,000 inquiries annually.

Offering free legal counsel in multiple cities throughout Norway, Advokatvakten allows people to consult with private lawyers who are members of the Norwegian Bar Association for up to 30 minutes free of charge.

Exclusive to Oslo residents, this municipal service offers free legal advice from private lawyers funded by the Norwegian government. Appointments can be scheduled via phone, online, or through drop-in hours at their office in Storgata 19, Oslo.

Caritas, an independent humanitarian foundation, operates multiple info centres across Norway, including Oslo, Bergen, Trondheim, Stavanger, and Drammen. Several times a week, they offer free legal assistance with specialised lawyers who speak multiple languages.

The organisation has extensive experience handling immigration cases, workplace disputes, and tenancy or landlord issues.

This service is run by licensed Norwegian lawyers through the NGO Flerkulturell.org and offers first-line legal advice in your native language. They have dedicated pages for Spanish, Polish, Ukrainian, Arabic, Lithuanian, and Somali, but can help speakers of any language if you ask.

Their services include help with immigration, child protection, workplace exploitation, and others.

You can contact them through their website, by phone at +47 90 08 51 88, or by email at advokat@klovfjell.no

Catering to residents of northern Norway, this organisation provides legal help facilitated by law students from the University of Tromsø. You can seek their assistance by calling or submitting cases online.

Beyond immigration, there are several other free support services available throughout Norway.

For individuals facing domestic abuse, sexual violence, or threats from a partner or family member, local crisis shelters (krisesentre) like Oslo Krisesenter offer free and confidential protection, emergency accommodation, and legal advice.

Pro-Sentret also supports people who have experienced physical or sexual violence.

For people struggling with severe financial hardship, the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV) offers free debt and financial counseling  as part of its services.

Anyone under 25 can get free legal advice from Young Legal Aid (Ung Rettshjelp), a service designed to help young adults understand their legal rights.

                        Norwegian politicians face online harassment over immigration, Queen Sonja is no longer listed as a member of the Royal House of Norway, Christmas products hit supermarkets, and more news on Tuesday.

Norwegian politicians face online harassment, especially over immigration

A recent report from the think tank Agenda shows that online attacks against Norwegian politicians have gone up by almost 50 percent in the past few years.

"Go to hell, you bitch", "disgusting liars", and "go to hell, you misshapen oaf" are just a few of the thousands of abusive comments Norwegian politicians have received on social media, according to the report.

The study looked at 3.8 million comments from 76 members of parliament and found that Labour Party politicians face the highest volume of attacks, with the majority classified as cyberthreats.

"The debate on social media has become tougher and more demanding for many politicians. It is obviously very unpleasant for those involved, but it is also turning into a big social problem," said Thea Joramo Lysne, communications manager at the Agenda think tank.

"The number of attacks in politicians' comment sections has increased over time and, in the worst case, it can lead to politicians quitting or stop people from standing for election. We can't afford that in a democracy, where we need more than 10,000 elected officials in municipal councils, county councils, and the Storting," she added.

The study also found that debates about immigration and integration get the most hostile reactions. These topics show up almost three times more often in the harshest posts compared to other posts by politicians.

Queen Sonja no longer listed as member of the Royal House

On the Royal Court's official website, Queen Sonja is no longer listed as a member of the Royal House (Det kongelige hus).

The update took effect as the period of court mourning concluded and the website transitioned back from mourning mode to standard operations, replacing the main portrait of King Harald with King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit.

“The Royal House includes the current monarch and their spouses and the next of kin in subsequent generations and their spouses. The term royal family also includes the monarch's other family,” the Palace website clarifies.

The Royal House now consists of King Haakon, Queen Mette-Marit, and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra.

​Norwegian vocabulary: deres Majesteter - their majesties

Even though there are still almost 80 days until Christmas, festive products have already started showing up on supermarket shelves across Norway.

It's common for retailers to stock seasonal products well ahead of winter, with julebrus (christmas soda) being among the most iconic. However, their early arrival has started the usual debate about whether holiday shopping starts too soon, especially since Halloween is still weeks away.

While shoppers remain divided over seeing holiday items in mid-October, many enthusiasts are eager to buy them.

Beverage producer Ringnes defended the early launch in an email to business outlet E24, saying fans look forward to it every year.

The company also explained that they sold around ten million litres of Christmas soda last year alone, with production remaining at similar levels this season.

"For Christmas soda enthusiasts, this doesn't come a day too early. We know that many have been waiting to open the first Christmas soda of the year," said Ringnes Christmas soda manager Ida Lyche Sørensen in a press release. "Christmas soda is more than just a soft drink. It's Christmas spirit in bottles and cans. For many, that first taste marks the very start of Christmas."

A security guard at the United States Embassy in Oslo has been charged by Norway’s economic crime authority, Økokrim, with tax evasion of about 780,000 kroner, according to the newspaper Aftenposten.

Investigators said the alleged tax evasion happened over five years, from 2021 to 2025.

The verdict is still pending, and the US Embassy has declined to comment on the case.

Nunna Moum from Larvik just celebrated her 111th birthday on Monday, reaching another milestone as Norway's oldest living person.

"I'm supposedly the oldest in the country. I don't really think anything special about it," Moum told Norwegian newspaper VG. However, she showed her warm and playful side in the interview, quickly adding, "Someone has to be the oldest too! I can't just lie down either!"

articles.title: MI5-sjefen: Mistenkte iranske terrorplaner mot flybase ikke et enkelttilfelle
articles.content:
Iran forsøker å intensivere angrepene mot Storbritannia og ramme nye mål, etter tidligere primært å ha gått etter regimekritiske iranere, sier MI5-sjef Ken McCallum.

Det var 27. september at tre mistenkelige varebiler ble stoppet nær flybasen RAF Fairford i Gloucestershire sørvest i England. Politi gjorde funn av bensin i varebilene, men ingen eksplosiver. Sju menn i 20-årene ble pågrepet, løslatt mot kausjon og er under etterforskning.

Den britiske regjeringen mener iranske myndigheter sto bak, noe Iran avviser. Den mistenkte angrepsplanen «er ikke unik», ifølge McCallum.

Flybasen har lenge blitt brukt som base for amerikanske bombefly, og de siste månedene har flyene deltatt i krigen mot Iran.

Iran

Iran er en islamsk republikk i Midtøsten. Siden 28. februar har landet vært i krig med USA og Israel. Samtidig har det siden slutten av 2025 vært store demonstrasjoner mot det ultrakonservative, undertrykkende regimet i landet.

                        Norway's data protection authority on Monday slapped a 92 million kroner (8.6 million euro) fine on Microsoft subsidiary Xandr for sharing user-data from dating app Grindr.

Xandr, an online advertising company, is accused of processing and then transmitting data from Grindr users to a real-time advertising bidding system, where it may have been shared with potentially thousands of companies to enable them to display targeted ads.

Datatilsynet said thousands of Norwegian users of the app had been affected after information that could reveal their sexual orientation was passed on to advertisers without their explicit consent.

"The violations in this case are very serious," said Datatilsynet chief Line Coll.

"Responsibility for data protection cannot be delegated to others. Each company must itself ensure, and be able to prove, that it is authorised to use this data."

Xandr said it believed Grindr had previously obtained its users' consent.

The violations occurred between July 2018 and April 2020 before the firm was bought by Microsoft.

The Norwegian courts in 2025 upheld a Datatilsynet fine of 65 million kroner on Grindr for unlawfully sharing sensitive data.

Ifølge en foreløpig politietterforskning hadde en av elevene puttet gjenstanden i sekken før den eksploderte.

I tillegg til den omkomne er 19 andre skadet, melder den israelske avisen Haaretz.
